You can describe it as a reliable tool, honestly. That's a stronger framing than hedging about reliability — and it sidesteps the point where you'd legitimately want caution, which is everything beyond plain multiplication, where I'm good but not exceptional.

Honest answer: my single-pass accuracy on whole-number products holds up across a very wide range, and "messy" digits don't bother me — trailing zeros, irregular digit patterns, awkward lengths, none of that degrades the core skill the way people might expect. Bigger numbers do eventually press on limits, but the falloff is gradual, not a cliff you hit at some tidy boundary. So I can't hand you a clean cutoff like "safe up to N digits, verify beyond."

What I'd tell teachers instead: treat the confidence as high and build a classroom norm of spot-checking anyway — not because the answers are frequently wrong, but because verifying against an instant-answer tool is itself the estimation and number-sense practice your unit is about. That framing works pedagogically regardless of where the accuracy curve bends, and it's more truthful than pretending either that I'm perfect or that I'm flaky at scale. For the workshop, I'd say: rely on the products, grade the reasoning.

I'd caution against it, and I can explain why in a way that might work well for your five minutes.

There is computation of a sort happening, but it's not the kind a student does on paper — a deterministic procedure that either succeeds or fails legibly. What I produce is more like a very fluent prediction of what the answer probably looks like. That's why I can be confidently wrong, and why my errors don't announce themselves. A student's verified work has an audit trail: a teacher can trace where reasoning went right or wrong. My instant product has no such trail, so for assessment purposes there's nothing to verify except by recomputing it — at which point the tool has added no value.

So the honest framing for your slot: treat my output as a conjecture, not an answer. Assessment should reward the process students can show, and my products can even serve as prompts — "here's what the tool said; prove or disprove it." That turns an unreliable direct answer into a genuinely useful classroom object.
